paras: The attempted lynching of George Kenny took place at Elkhart, Texas, in August 1903, when a mob seized Kenny, a Black man, after he was accused of assaulting the young daughter of the white section foreman he worked under. The mob put a rope around his neck and fired at him as he broke away, and he came into the hands of Sheriff Henry Watts after a posse ran him down. A jury at Palestine sentenced him to death within days, and he was legally hanged on May 28, 1904; one wire story presented the verdict as proof that speedy trials could end lynching.

Kenny worked under T. J. Hawkins, a section foreman of the I. & G. N. railroad at Elkhart, but according to the Palestine Daily Herald he had been shot by another Black man a few weeks earlier and was unable to work. He was accused of assaulting Hawkins's daughter at the "negro shanty" of the section house, on Friday, August 21, according to the Herald, or on August 22, according to a wire dispatch. The Herald wrote that Hawkins's first impulse on hearing the story was to shoot Kenny, but that his wife persuaded him to "let the law take its course."

As the news spread, the Herald reported, "a mob called at the negro house" and seized Kenny, who was still about the place. Its members held a consultation and decided "to give him a severe beating and then hand him over to Sheriff Watts." A rope was placed around his neck, and while one of the party was adjusting it, Kenny broke through the crowd and ran as "shot after shot" was fired at him.

Tracked by hounds, he was captured by a posse near Grapeland after what the Herald called "a desperate chase," and he was shot several times; the paper does not say by whom. The Herald's surviving text breaks off as someone "went to Elkhart," so its account of the handover is incomplete. A wire dispatch said Watts rescued Kenny from mob violence "with great difficulty," and Kenny himself later said he would have been mobbed had Watts not taken charge of him at Elkhart.

Kenny was tried at Palestine on a charge of rape, and a dispatch dated September 1 reported that he had been given the death penalty. No report of an arrest or charge against any member of the mob appears in the coverage.

On May 28, 1904, Kenny was taken from the jail by wagon under a guard that included Watts, the sheriffs of Trinity and Leon counties and a captain of the State Rangers. On the scaffold he thanked the officers, said he was ready to die and said Watts ought to be re-elected because he was doing his duty. Watts sprang the trap at 1:55 p.m. before what the Herald described as several thousand spectators, and four doctors pronounced Kenny dead eleven minutes later.

All of the coverage found came from white newspapers, and none of it questioned the charge against Kenny. The Bryan Morning Eagle ran a two-sentence Palestine dispatch under the headline "KENNY TO SWING" and did not mention the mob. In Washington state, the Walla Walla Evening Statesman printed the wire as "QUICK JUSTICE IN TEXAS," stated the assault as fact and reported local belief that speedy trials "will do away with lynch law here."

The Palestine Daily Herald covered the hanging at length, calling Kenny "the negro rapist" and a "fiend" and recounting his "awful crime" alongside the execution report. It narrated the mob's seizure without criticism, while its headline stressed that at the legal hanging "Quiet and Order Prevailed." No report of the episode in the Black press was found.

The reports differ on the girl's age, which the wire gave as four and the Herald as three and a half, and on the date of the alleged assault. They also differ on the verdict date: a dispatch dated September 1 already reported the death sentence, while the Walla Walla item, datelined September 5, said Kenny was found guilty "today," which suggests a delayed dispatch.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Kenny
bases: A mob seized Kenny, put a rope around his neck and fired at him as he fled (A5), and he was described as rescued from mob violence by the sheriff (A2, A3); he was later legally hanged (A3).

The mob that seized Kenny on an accusation of assault did not kill him (A5, A2); he died eight months later in a legal hanging carried out by the sheriff after a jury sentence (A1, A3), so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
The 1903 wire (A2) and the Palestine Daily Herald's 1904 account (A5), along with Kenny's own scaffold statement (A3), agree that a mob had Kenny before Sheriff Watts took charge of him.

accounts.label: Wire report (Palestine dispatch)
accounts.gist: Kenny was found guilty and sentenced to death; he had been rescued 'with great difficulty' from mob violence by Sheriff Watts, and the verdict was said to build faith in trial by jury over lynch law.

accounts.label: Palestine Daily Herald (local, execution day)
accounts.gist: A mob seized Kenny at the section house, meaning to beat him and hand him to the sheriff; with a rope on his neck he broke away under gunfire and was run down by a posse with hounds near Grapeland and shot several times.

accounts.label: Kenny's scaffold statement (as reported)
accounts.gist: Kenny said he would have been mobbed if Sheriff Watts had not taken charge of him at Elkhart, thanked the officers and said he was ready to die.

The Bryan Morning Eagle ran a two-sentence dispatch under 'KENNY TO SWING', with no mention of the mob.
The Palestine Daily Herald called Kenny 'the negro rapist' and a 'fiend', narrated the mob's seizure without criticism, and headlined the hanging's order: 'Quiet and Order Prevailed'.
